ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Screen all direct and indirect owners, directors, officers, authorized signatories, controllers, major counterparties, and payment beneficiaries before incorporation and periodically thereafter against Canadian sanctions lists administered under the United Nations Act, Special Economic Measures Act, and Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act; UN Security Council sanctions; OFAC SDN and relevant non-SDN lists where a United States nexus exists; and reputable commercial PEP, relatives-and-close-associates, adverse-media, and vessel or entity screening databases. The PCMLTFA and its regulations impose mandatory PEP and beneficial-ownership controls primarily on reporting entities, including banks, certain payment service providers, money services businesses, securities dealers, and other listed businesses. An ordinary AdTech corporation is not automatically a PCMLTFA reporting entity solely because it receives Swift wires or ACH payments, but Canadian banks and payment providers will apply their own AML, sanctions, source-of-funds, source-of-wealth, and tax-residency controls. Escalate unresolved matches, obtain documentary evidence, prohibit transactions with sanctioned persons, and retain screening records under the applicable institution policy and law.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Corporations Canada Online Filing Centre, administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED); federal word-name searches generally use a NUANS corporate name search report obtained through an authorized NUANS service provider
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: A federal corporation may use an English, French, or bilingual corporate name. The corporate name must comply with the Canada Business Corporations Act and Regulations, be distinctive, and not be confusing with an existing corporate name, business name, or trademark. A corporate name may contain French and English elements. Non-Latin characters and transliterations require registry and technical acceptance and should be supported by a compliant Roman-alphabet version. A numbered corporation is available where a word name is unavailable or unsuitable. Name clearance is separate from trademark clearance and provincial extra-provincial registration.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Words implying a regulated financial, insurance, educational, governmental, or professional status without the required statutory authorization
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: Obtain a current NUANS report before filing where a word name is proposed. A NUANS report is generally valid for 90 days; federal incorporation filings should be submitted within that period. If Corporations Canada rejects the proposed name, obtain the written reason, compare the name against the Canada Business Corporations Act, Canada Business Corporations Regulations, NUANS results, and Canadian trademark databases, and submit a revised name or supporting consent and evidence of distinctiveness through the Online Filing Centre. A statutory administrative appeal is not ordinarily available as an automatic appeal from a routine name rejection. Escalate a disputed decision by written request for reconsideration to Corporations Canada, supported by evidence of consent, prior use, non-confusion, or authorization; seek judicial review in the Federal Court under the Federal Courts Act if an appealable administrative decision is unreasonable, procedurally unfair, or unlawful. Name approval does not establish trademark rights and does not eliminate provincial registration requirements.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: A federal corporation must maintain a registered office in the province or territory specified in its articles under the Canada Business Corporations Act, including a real physical address where legal documents may be served; a post-office box alone is insufficient. A commercial virtual-office provider may be acceptable for a low-regulatory AdTech platform if it supplies a genuine service address, mail handling, record access, and reliable service-of-process procedures. The corporation should maintain Canadian corporate records, accounting records, tax records, contracts, payment documentation, and evidence of actual management and operating activity. A virtual office does not by itself establish Canadian tax residence, treaty residence, transfer-pricing substance, or eligibility for treaty benefits.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Estimated 1%-5% annual probability of an unannounced physical inspection for a standard low-risk AdTech corporation with consistent filings, ordinary commercial activity, and no regulatory red flags; this is a non-statutory risk estimate, not an official government statistic. Risk may materially increase following suspicious transaction indicators, inconsistent beneficial-ownership information, tax non-compliance, sanctions concerns, consumer complaints, registered-office failures, or a request from a bank, FINTRAC, CRA, or law-enforcement agency. The company should be able to demonstrate accessible records and credible Canadian management and operations.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency / Agence du revenu du Canada (CRA); online portal: CRA My Business Account — https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency.html
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign entity carrying on business in Canada must first obtain a statutory Business Number (BN) via CRA Business Registration Online (BRO) or by filing a paper application with the relevant tax services office. The BN, supplemented by program accounts, functions as the Canadian corporate TIN. For federal corporation income tax, the non-resident entity must register for an RC program account and file a T2 return if it carries on business in Canada. For GST/HST, the entity must register for an RT program account through the same BN process when it is not a small supplier (i.e. worldwide taxable supply revenue exceeds C$30,000) and makes taxable supplies from or in Canada. Non-resident digital service suppliers may use CRA's simplified GST/HST registration procedure. The CRA requires certified corporate documents from the foreign jurisdiction, registered office/agent details, and evidence of authority for the Canadian representative.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: Canada does not maintain a check-the-box or pass-through election regime. A corporation incorporated federally is a resident taxpayer by default and is taxed at the entity level on worldwide income, subject to treaty tie-breaker rules. Non-resident corporations are taxed on Canadian-source income with no elective classification override. Hybrid mismatch rules under Income Tax Act s. 18.6 may deny deductions involving hybrid entities or hybrid transfers and do not provide elective carve-outs. Limited statutory elections exist for fiscal period selection under s. 249.1 and for certain Part I returns by non-residents, but none alter entity-level tax treatment.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) / Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) — federal value-added tax with provincial harmonization
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: C$30,000 in worldwide gross revenue from taxable supplies (small supplier threshold); compulsory GST/HST registration if a non-resident carries on business in Canada and exceeds this threshold. Non-resident digital economy suppliers to Canadian consumers are subject to simplified registration with a similar C$30,000 Canadian-source revenue threshold.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not mandate real-time fiscal clearance, digital stamping, or a national continuous transaction control (CTC) system. E-invoices are accepted for GST/HST compliance provided they satisfy CRA record retention requirements. GST/HST returns are filed electronically through CRA Business Number portals. PEPPOL standards may apply to public-sector e-procurement, but this is procurement interoperability, not a tax clearance requirement.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: A supply of programmatic ad exchange/SSP services to a non-resident recipient is zero-rated under the Excise Tax Act, Schedule VI, Part V, section 7 if the recipient is not registered under GST/HST and the service is not in respect of real property in Canada, tangible personal property situated in Canada, or intangible personal property for use in Canada. Services delivered electronically from Canada to foreign trade counterparties with documented non-resident counterparties generally qualify. Goods exports are eligible for zero-rating when the supplier exports the goods on a shipment-by-shipment basis and retains prescribed documentary proof declared to CRA.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: For goods: CBSA Export Declaration (Form B13A) or eManifest export declaration number
Bill of Lading / Airway Bill or Cargo Control Document
Bank payment evidence (SWIFT MT103, FX conversion confirmation, or inward remittance certificate)
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA audits may test whether the entity has contemporaneous proof of foreign provision, foreign non-registration status, and payment for exported services. Missing documentation or payment received after the 180-day benchmark without commercial justification can cause zero-rating to be denied, leading to reassessment, interest, cancellation of input tax credits, and potential clawback of refunds. Penalties for false statements under the Excise Tax Act can be up to 25% of the tax at issue, gross-negligence penalties up to 50%, and willful evasion may result in criminal fines and imprisonment.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (Banque du Canada) as the monetary authority and issuance entity for the Canadian dollar; prudential supervision of deposit-taking institutions is conducted by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI). Canada does not maintain a dedicated foreign-exchange administration or exchange-control authority.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is fully convertible for both current-account and capital-account transactions under Article VIII of the IMF Articles of Agreement. Canada imposes no foreign-exchange controls, no capital-account approval thresholds for inward equity investment, and no restrictions on maintaining foreign-currency deposits in Canadian Schedule I banks or on repatriating profits abroad. Profit remittance frictions are purely tax and compliance driven: a 25% Part XIII dividend withholding tax under the Income Tax Act (generally reduced to 0-15% under an applicable income tax treaty), the anti-money-laundering and large-transaction reporting obligations under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA), and sanctions screening requirements applicable to all OSFI-regulated financial institutions. None of these frictions abridge the lawful convertibility of CAD or the free movement of capital.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Statutory timeline: not applicable. Mandatory conversion ratio: none. Canada does not impose any export-proceeds surrender, forced conversion, or minimum holding period for foreign-currency receipts. The Canadian entity may retain export revenues in CAD or any foreign currency, in Canada or abroad, indefinitely. For this AdTech DSP/SSP programmatic advertising platform, cross-border revenue from foreign exchanges and demand sources is not subject to repatriation timing rules. The only applicable duties are general tax filing obligations (foreign accrual rules, GST/HST on Canadian services) and PCMLTFA reporting thresholds for transactions of CAD 10,000 or more.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Low as a primary treasury repository, Medium as a supplementary payment-facilitation rail. Legal constraints: there is no EU-style Electronic Money Institution (EMI) regime in Canada, and no offshore EMI passporting arrangement exists. An offshore digital EMI cannot lawfully take deposits or issue electronic money in Canada unless it is authorized by OSFI or properly registered as a Money Services Business (MSB) with FINTRAC under PCMLTFA, and, depending on the province, licensed as an MSB by the Autorité des marchés financiers (AMF) in Quebec or under the Money Services Business Act in British Columbia. Reliance on an unregistered offshore EMI for main operating liquidity is inadvisable: Canadian clearing banks will typically reject or suspend transfers sourced from unregulated payment intermediaries. The recommended architecture uses a foreign EMI only for small-value cross-border receipts, with all material balances swept to a Schedule I Canadian bank account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: No federal statute mandates physical attendance by directors for account opening. FINTRAC Client Due Diligence rules permit remote onboarding where the bank applies enhanced verification, including video-based identity verification, public-record database checks, and certified documentary evidence. In practical Canadian market practice, Schedule I banks will require a live video compliance interview for at least one director plus the ultimate beneficial owner, a complete corporate KYC pack, and proof of Canadian substance (registered office, directors' residency profile, or local professional advisors). Fully remote opening is possible at certain banks, but the prudent blueprint is hybrid: electronic submission of the corporate and beneficial-ownership dossier followed by a scheduled video interview, with an in-person branch meeting only if the bank's regional risk policy mandates it.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident beneficial ownership concentrated in an offshore parent group or presented through nominee directors
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: CBCA Articles of Incorporation, Initial Notice of Directors and Annual Return, Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) Register required by s. 21.1 of the Canada Business Corporations Act, full beneficial-ownership legal-entity chart, attested passport and proof-of-address for every owner, a banking reference from the existing parent-company bank, board resolutions approving the Canadian entity's treasury mandate, and evidence of Canadian economic substance (lease, payroll, professional service agreements).

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: AdTech platform generating high-volume small-ticket transactions which may resemble anonymized online payments or mixed-purpose receivables
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: A signed commercial and technical description of the programmatic Ad Exchange, DSP and SSP model, executed agreements with DSPs, SSPs, ad exchanges and data suppliers, sample invoices and settlement statements, monthly projected transaction volumes in CAD and USD, historical fintech or banking ledger evidence showing a consistent revenue pattern, and a written undertaking to provide periodic transaction-level reporting to the commercial account officer.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-velocity outbound disbursements to non-resident vendors and media counterparties creating invoice-factoring or trade-based money-laundering suspicion
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Counterparty-KYC schedule containing the legal name, jurisdiction, and SWIFT beneficiary details of each expected payee, underlying media-buying and API-services contracts, invoice-backed payment substantiation, an FX disbursement forecast, and a board-approved treasury policy defining payment authorization limits and segregation of duties.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Potential classification of the entity as a Money Services Business or unlicensed payment intermediary where the platform processes payments for sub-publishers or performs foreign-exchange conversion for third parties
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Legal opinion confirming that the Canadian corporation transacts for its own account in buying and selling advertising inventory and does not provide money-transfer, currency-exchange, or payment-processing services to unrelated merchants. If the facts support MSB activity, the defense requires a FINTRAC MSB registration certificate, provincial licensing documentation (Quebec AMF or British Columbia MSBA), a fully documented AML compliance program, and a named AML Compliance Officer, all submitted before account activation.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity funding is routed by SWIFT MT103 wire from the parent or shareholder's bank to the Corporation's Canadian bank account. The wire's field 70 remittance information should state 'Equity Capital Contribution' or 'Share Subscription - CAD' to differentiate the injection from trading revenue. No foreign-investment authorization, exchange-control permit, or regulatory pre-approval is required in Canada for a non-resident capital injection. CAD-denominated settlement occurs over Lynx, Payments Canada's real-time gross settlement system, or a correspondent bank's overnight clearing arrangement. The receiving bank must verify the remitter's identity and source of funds; wires of CAD 10,000 or more are reported to FINTRAC. For injections exceeding CAD 100,000, the bank will typically require a board resolution, the subscription agreement, pro forma financial statements, and a director's certificate confirming the corporate capacity of the recipient.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade and vendor disbursements are executed through SWIFT MT103 high-value wires for non-resident counterparties, cleared via the correspondent banking network, using CHIPS or Fedwire for USD and Lynx for CAD; recurring small-value payments to US sub-publishers and data vendors are effected through ACH (US ACH for USD, ACSS Automated Clearing Settlement Service for CAD). Commercial Letters of Credit (documentary LC under UCP600) and standby LCs are permissible for material media-acquisition contracts requiring documentary security. Each outbound payment should include the invoice number and campaign reference in the remittance field, and the beneficiary's full BIC/SWIFT, account number or IBAN, and clearing address must be validated to prevent misdirection. The blueprint segments the payment rails: CAD operating disbursements via ACSS/Lynx, USD vendor settlements via MT103 over a USD correspondent account, and sponsor-media or inventory acquisitions via LC only when contractually required by the non-resident counterparty.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: CAD/USD foreign-exchange swaps (tom-next, spot-next and forward swaps)
CAD/USD vanilla options (calls and puts) transacted with a licensed Canadian bank or registered derivatives dealer

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for CAD are not a permissible onshore hedging instrument given the full convertibility of the Canadian dollar; any offshore NDF usage is excluded from the authorized treasury policy

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under the Canada Business Corporations Act
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada, Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within 60 days after the corporation's anniversary date of incorporation, amalgamation, or continuance; file annually through the Corporations Canada online system.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: The prescribed fee is CAD 12 for online filing. Continued non-filing may result in a compliance notice and administrative dissolution, generally after two consecutive annual returns remain outstanding; restoration requires an application, prescribed fees, and updated filings.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: A federal corporation must appoint an auditor unless the corporation qualifies as a non-distributing corporation and all shareholders unanimously consent annually to waive the audit requirement. A distributing corporation must maintain an auditor and comply with applicable public-company financial statement requirements. No revenue, asset, or employee threshold independently triggers a CBCA audit.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Canadian Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. Publicly accountable enterprises generally apply IFRS as adopted in Canada; eligible private enterprises may apply Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises under Part II of the CPA Canada Handbook.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Maintain an Individuals with Significant Control register at the registered office. Review it at least annually and after every share transfer or ownership, control, or identifying-information change. File the required individuals-with-significant-control information with Corporations Canada through the annual return and report changes within 15 days where required by the Canada Business Corporations Act.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Minute Book containing shareholder and director resolutions and meeting minutes

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: Typically USD 300-1,200 annually, excluding provincial extra-provincial registrations, mail handling, nominee services, and special filings.
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: Typically USD 2,000-10,000 for a small private corporation; higher fees apply to distributing corporations, complex AdTech platforms, related-party structures, material revenue recognition issues, or multi-jurisdictional operations.
